blocks.body:
Every whole number is a sum of four squares, every large odd number is a sum of three primes, and every positive integer is a sum of distinct powers of $2$. Each of these says that a fairly sparse set of integers still generates all (or almost all) integers by addition, using a bounded number of summands or using each element at most once.

This lesson sets up the language, explains the counting and congruence obstructions, proves Schnirelmann's density theorem and Brown's criterion for completeness, and ends with the Erdős–Turán conjecture of 1941, still open, about how evenly a basis must spread its representations.

blocks.title: Bases of finite order
blocks.body:
Throughout, $A$ is a set of nonnegative integers and $hA = \{a_1+\cdots+a_h : a_i \in A\}$ is its $h$-fold sumset, as in [[additive-combinatorics]] (repetitions allowed). We write $A(x) = \#\{a \in A : 1 \le a \le x\}$ for the counting function.

It is convenient to put $0$ in $A$. Then "a sum of exactly $h$ elements of $A$" and "a sum of at most $h$ nonzero elements of $A$" mean the same thing, which is how the classical theorems are usually phrased. For example, with $Q = \{0,1,4,9,16,\dots\}$, the statement $7 \notin 3Q$ says that $7$ is not a sum of at most three positive squares.

The quantity that measures how many ways $n$ is generated is the representation function. For two summands, as in the key statement,
$$r_A(n) = \#\{(a,b) \in A^2 : a + b = n\},$$
counting ordered pairs; similarly $r_{A,h}(n)$ counts ordered $h$-tuples. So $n \in hA$ exactly when $r_{A,h}(n) \ge 1$.

blocks.title: Basis of order h; complete sequence
blocks.body:
A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ is an (asymptotic) basis of order $h$ if every sufficiently large integer $n$ lies in $hA$, that is, $r_{A,h}(n) \ge 1$ for all $n \ge n_0$. It is a basis of finite order if it is a basis of order $h$ for some $h$.

A set or sequence $A$ of positive integers is complete if every sufficiently large integer is a sum of distinct elements of $A$ (a finite subset sum).

A basis lets you reuse elements a bounded number of times; completeness forbids repetition but allows unboundedly many summands.

blocks.title: Two obstructions: counting and congruences
blocks.body:
Counting. If $A$ is a basis of order $h$, the sums of $h$ elements of $A \cap [0,x]$ must cover all integers in $[n_0, x]$. There are at most $(A(x)+1)^h$ such ordered sums (the $+1$ accounts for $0$), so
$$(A(x)+1)^h \ge x - n_0 + 1,\qquad\text{hence}\qquad A(x) \ge c\,x^{1/h}$$
for some $c > 0$ and all large $x$. A basis of order $h$ cannot be much thinner than the $h$-th powers. The squares have $A(x) \approx \sqrt{x}$, so counting alone would allow order $2$.

Congruences. Counting is not the whole story. A square is $0$ or $1$ modulo $4$, so a sum of two squares is never $3 \bmod 4$; the squares are not a basis of order $2$. A square is $0$, $1$ or $4$ modulo $8$, and three of these never add to $7 \bmod 8$, so no $n \equiv 7 \pmod 8$ is a sum of three squares. Since $4m$ is a sum of three squares only when $m$ is (all three squares must then be even), every number $4^a(8b+7)$ fails. Infinitely many integers are not in $3Q$, so the squares are not a basis of order $3$ either.

These two obstructions, size and local (congruence) conditions, are the first things to check for any proposed basis. For the squares, order $4$ is where both disappear.

blocks.title: Classical bases
blocks.body:
1. (Lagrange, 1770) The squares $Q$ form a basis of order $4$; in fact $4Q = \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.
2. (Hilbert, 1909; Waring's problem) For each $k \ge 2$ the $k$-th powers $\{0, 1, 2^k, 3^k, \dots\}$ form a basis of finite order.
3. (Schnirelmann, around 1930) The set $\{0,1\} \cup \{\text{primes}\}$ is a basis of finite order: there is a constant $C$ such that every integer $n \ge 2$ is a sum of at most $C$ primes.
4. (Vinogradov, 1937) Every sufficiently large odd integer is a sum of three primes. Consequently $\{0\} \cup \{\text{primes}\}$ is a basis of order $4$: an even $n$ is $3$ plus an odd number.

The proofs of 2 and 4 use the circle method; see [[waring]] and [[ternary-goldbach]]. Goldbach's conjecture ([[goldbach]]) would say that every even number $n \ge 4$ is a sum of two primes.

blocks.title: Schnirelmann density
blocks.body:
Schnirelmann found an elementary route to statements like item 3: measure the size of $A$ by
$$\sigma(A) = \inf_{n \ge 1} \frac{A(n)}{n}.$$
This is a harsh density: if $1 \notin A$ then $A(1) = 0$ and $\sigma(A) = 0$, and a single missing initial stretch lowers it permanently. But it has a clean behaviour under addition, proved below, which turns positive density into a finite-order basis.

The primes themselves have $\sigma = 0$ (they have density zero), so the theorem is not applied to them directly. Schnirelmann instead showed, with a sieve upper bound for the number of representations of $n$ as $p+q$ (see [[sieve-basics]]), that the set of numbers that are sums of two primes, together with $0$ and $1$, has positive Schnirelmann density. The theorem below then finishes the job. We omit the sieve part.

blocks.title: Schnirelmann's inequality
blocks.body:
If $0 \in A$ and $0 \in B$, then
$$\sigma(A+B) \ge \sigma(A) + \sigma(B) - \sigma(A)\sigma(B),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad 1-\sigma(A+B) \le (1-\sigma(A))(1-\sigma(B)).$$
Moreover, if $\sigma(A) + \sigma(B) \ge 1$, then $A + B$ contains every nonnegative integer.

blocks.title: Proof of Schnirelmann's inequality
blocks.body:
Fix $n \ge 1$, let $\alpha = \sigma(A)$, $\beta = \sigma(B)$, and list the elements of $A$ in $[1,n]$ as $a_1 < \cdots < a_k$, so $k = A(n) \ge \alpha n$. Put $a_0 = 0$ and $a_{k+1} = n+1$. The gaps $g_i = a_{i+1} - a_i - 1$ ($0 \le i \le k$) count the integers of $[1,n]$ strictly between consecutive elements, so $\sum_i g_i = n - k$.

Every $a_j$ is in $A+B$ because $0 \in B$. Inside the $i$-th gap, every number $a_i + b$ with $b \in B$ and $1 \le b \le g_i$ is in $A+B$ (for $i = 0$ this uses $0 \in A$). These numbers lie strictly between $a_i$ and $a_{i+1}$, so all the numbers listed are distinct, and the $i$-th gap contributes $B(g_i) \ge \beta g_i$ of them. Hence
$$(A+B)(n) \ge k + \beta(n-k) = k(1-\beta) + \beta n \ge \alpha n(1-\beta) + \beta n.$$
Dividing by $n$ and taking the infimum gives $\sigma(A+B) \ge \alpha + \beta - \alpha\beta$.

For the second claim, let $n \ge 1$; if $n \in A$ or $n \in B$ we are done (add $0$). Otherwise $A(n-1) = A(n) \ge \alpha n$ and $B(n-1) = B(n) \ge \beta n$. The sets $\{a \in A: 1 \le a \le n-1\}$ and $\{n - b : b \in B,\ 1 \le b \le n-1\}$ both lie in $[1, n-1]$ and have total size at least $(\alpha+\beta)n \ge n > n-1$, so they share an element $a = n - b$. Thus $n = a + b \in A + B$. Finally $0 = 0 + 0$.

blocks.title: From positive density to a basis
blocks.body:
Iterating the inequality with $B = A, 2A, \dots$ gives $1 - \sigma(hA) \le (1-\sigma(A))^h$. If $\sigma(A) > 0$, choose $h$ with $(1-\sigma(A))^h \le \tfrac12$; then $\sigma(hA) \ge \tfrac12$, and the second part of the theorem applied to $hA + hA$ shows $2hA = \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$. So:

If $0 \in A$ and $\sigma(A) > 0$, then every nonnegative integer is a sum of $2h$ elements of $A$, that is $2hA = \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, with $h$ depending only on $\sigma(A)$.

Mann (1942) later proved the sharper $\sigma(A+B) \ge \min(1, \sigma(A)+\sigma(B))$, which Schnirelmann and Landau had conjectured. We do not prove it.

blocks.title: Completeness and Brown's criterion
blocks.body:
Completeness is the "distinct summands" version. The powers of $2$ are complete (binary expansion); so are the Fibonacci numbers $1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots$ (Zeckendorf). Computation and some care show that every integer greater than $128$ is a sum of distinct squares (a result of Sprague, 1948), and every integer greater than $6$ is a sum of distinct primes (Richert, 1949). The exceptions are genuine: $128$ is not a sum of distinct squares, and $1, 4, 6$ are not sums of distinct primes.

For sequences that start at $1$, there is a clean test.

blocks.title: Brown's criterion
blocks.body:
Let $a_1 \le a_2 \le a_3 \le \cdots$ be positive integers with $a_1 = 1$. Every positive integer is a sum of distinct terms $a_i$ (distinct indices) if and only if
$$a_{k+1} \le 1 + a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_k \qquad\text{for all } k \ge 1.$$

blocks.title: Proof of Brown's criterion
blocks.body:
Write $s_k = a_1 + \cdots + a_k$. If the inequality fails for some $k$, then $s_k + 1 < a_{k+1} \le a_{k+2} \le \cdots$, so the integer $s_k + 1$ cannot use any term from index $k+1$ on, and the first $k$ terms add up to at most $s_k$. It is not representable.

Conversely, assume the inequality and prove by induction on $k$ that every integer in $[1, s_k]$ is a sum of distinct terms among $a_1, \dots, a_k$. For $k = 1$ this is $[1,1]$. Suppose it holds for $k$ and let $s_k < m \le s_{k+1}$. Then $m - a_{k+1} \le s_k$, and $m - a_{k+1} \ge s_k + 1 - a_{k+1} \ge 0$ by the hypothesis. If $m - a_{k+1} = 0$ we are done; otherwise $m - a_{k+1} \in [1, s_k]$ is a sum of distinct terms among the first $k$, and adding $a_{k+1}$ represents $m$. Since $s_k \to \infty$, every positive integer is covered.

blocks.title: Squares are not a basis of order 3, and the counting bound
blocks.body:
(a) Show that no integer of the form $8b+7$ is a sum of three squares, and list those below $50$.

(b) Use the counting bound $A(x) \ge c\,x^{1/h}$ to show that the cubes $\{0, 1, 8, 27, \dots\}$ cannot be a basis of order $2$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Modulo $8$, $0^2,1^2,\dots,7^2$ are $0,1,4,1,0,1,4,1$, so a square is $0$, $1$ or $4 \bmod 8$. Sums of three elements of $\{0,1,4\}$ modulo $8$ give $0,1,2,3,4,5,6$ (for instance $3 = 1+1+1$, $6 = 1+1+4$) but never $7$. The integers $8b+7$ below $50$ are $7, 15, 23, 31, 39, 47$; none is a sum of three squares. (Also $28 = 4\cdot 7$ fails, by the halving argument in the text.)

(b) For the cubes, $A(x) = \lfloor x^{1/3} \rfloor$, and the number of sums of two elements of $A \cap [0,x]$ is at most $(x^{1/3}+1)^2$, about $x^{2/3}$, far less than the $x - n_0 + 1$ integers it would have to cover. So the cubes are not a basis of order $2$ — or of order $h = 3$ either, by a congruence argument modulo $9$ (cubes are $0, \pm 1 \bmod 9$, so a sum of three cubes is never $4$ or $5 \bmod 9$).

blocks.title: The representation function cannot be eventually constant
blocks.body: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ be infinite, and let $r_A(n)$ count ordered pairs as above. Show that $r_A(n)$ cannot be equal to a constant $c$ for all $n \ge n_0$.
blocks.solution:
The ordered pairs $(a,b)$ with $a+b=n$ come in swapped pairs $(a,b), (b,a)$, except the pair $(n/2, n/2)$, which exists exactly when $n$ is even and $n/2 \in A$. Hence
$$r_A(n) \equiv \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n \text{ is even and } n/2 \in A,\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} \pmod 2.$$

Suppose $r_A(n) = c$ for all $n \ge n_0$. If $c$ is even, then $n/2 \notin A$ for every even $n \ge n_0$, so $A$ has no element $\ge n_0/2$ and is finite, a contradiction. If $c$ is odd, then $m \in A$ for every $m \ge n_0/2$; but then for large $n$ the pairs $(a, n-a)$ with $n_0/2 \le a \le n - n_0/2$ all count, so $r_A(n) \ge n - n_0$, which is not constant. Either way we reach a contradiction.

This is the easy end of the Erdős–Turán problem below: a basis of order $2$ cannot have perfectly constant representation counts. Whether the counts can stay bounded is the open question.

blocks.title: Fibonacci numbers are complete
blocks.body: Let $F_1 = F_2 = 1$ and $F_{k+1} = F_k + F_{k-1}$. Use Brown's criterion to show that every positive integer is a sum of distinct terms of $1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \dots$ (that is, $F_2, F_3, F_4, \dots$), and represent $100$.
blocks.solution:
Set $a_k = F_{k+1}$, so $a_1 = 1, a_2 = 2, a_3 = 3, \dots$, nondecreasing with $a_1 = 1$. By induction $F_1 + \cdots + F_m = F_{m+2} - 1$ (true for $m = 1$, and adding $F_{m+1}$ to both sides gives $F_{m+3} - 1$). Hence
$$a_1 + \cdots + a_k = F_2 + \cdots + F_{k+1} = F_{k+3} - 1 - F_1 = F_{k+3} - 2.$$
Brown's condition asks $a_{k+1} = F_{k+2} \le F_{k+3} - 1$, which holds because $F_{k+3} - F_{k+2} = F_{k+1} \ge 1$. So the sequence is complete, in the strong sense that every positive integer is represented.

For $100$, take the largest term not exceeding what remains each time: $100 = 89 + 11 = 89 + 8 + 3$. (This greedy choice is exactly the Zeckendorf representation, which never uses two consecutive Fibonacci numbers.)

blocks.title: Thin bases and the Erdős–Turán conjecture
blocks.body:
How thin can a basis of order $2$ be? Counting forces $A(x) \gg \sqrt{x}$. Since $\sum_{n \le x} r_A(n) \le (A(x)+1)^2$, a basis with $A(x)$ of order exactly $\sqrt{x}$ has $r_A(n)$ bounded on average. One might hope for a basis with $r_A(n)$ bounded, a set that generates every integer but never too redundantly. Erdős and Turán (1941) conjectured that this is impossible:

If $r_A(n) \ge 1$ for all sufficiently large $n$, then $\limsup_{n\to\infty} r_A(n) = \infty$.

This is the key statement, and it is open. (Requiring $r_A(n) \ge 1$ for all $n$ or only for large $n$ makes no difference: adding finitely many elements to $A$ changes each $r_A(n)$ by a bounded amount.) The analogous conjecture for bases of order $h \ge 3$, that $r_{A,h}$ must be unbounded, is open as well.

In the other direction, Erdős proved by a probabilistic construction (see [[probabilistic-method]]) that there is a basis of order $2$ with $c_1 \log n \le r_A(n) \le c_2 \log n$ for all large $n$. Choose each $m$ to be in $A$ independently with probability about $\sqrt{\log m / m}$; the expected value of $r_A(n)$ is then of order $\log n$, and concentration inequalities show that, with probability $1$, every large $n$ has $r_A(n)$ within constant factors of its mean. So the truth lies between bounded and logarithmic, and nobody knows where.

The same circle of ideas meets [[sidon-sets]], where one asks for $r_A(n) \le 2$ for all $n$ (essentially all sums distinct): a Sidon set has $A(x) \ll \sqrt{x}$, the same order of magnitude as a basis must have, which is why the two problems pull against each other.

- Conventions vary: some authors count unordered representations, or require $a \le b$; the parity argument above is for ordered pairs. Always check which $r_A$ is meant.
- "Basis of order $h$" with $0 \notin A$ means exactly $h$ summands, which can fail for parity or size reasons even when "at most $h$" holds. Adding $0$ removes the distinction.
- Schnirelmann density is not natural density. The even numbers together with $0$ and $1$ have Schnirelmann density $\tfrac{1}{2}$, but the even numbers alone (without $1$) have Schnirelmann density $0$.
- Completeness is about distinct summands; the squares form a basis of order $4$, yet $128$ is not a sum of distinct squares.

Additive bases sit where [[additive-combinatorics]] meets analytic number theory. The circle method ([[circle-method]]) proves the strongest basis theorems, for [[waring]] and [[ternary-goldbach]], with precise asymptotics for $r_{A,h}(n)$; sieve methods ([[sieve-basics]]) give the upper bounds Schnirelmann needed. The tension between bases and [[sidon-sets]] is a recurring theme in [[combinatorial-nt]], and the representation-function questions lead naturally to the probabilistic constructions of [[probabilistic-method]]. Lagrange's theorem itself is part of the story of [[sums-of-squares]] and [[quadratic-forms]].

1. Show that $\{0\} \cup \{n : n \equiv 0 \text{ or } 1 \pmod 3\}$ is a basis of order $2$ and compute its Schnirelmann density.
2. Give a set $A$ containing $0$ and $1$, with at least one element in every interval $[2^k, 2^{k+1})$, that is not a basis of finite order. (Hint: compare with the counting bound.)
3. Let $1 = a_1 \le a_2 \le \cdots$ satisfy $a_{k+1} \le 2a_k$ for all $k$. Show that the sequence is complete, and deduce from Bertrand's postulate that $1$ together with the primes is complete.
4. Let $B$ be the set of nonnegative integers whose base-$4$ digits are all $0$ or $1$, and $C = \{2b : b \in B\}$. Show that every nonnegative integer is uniquely $b + c$ with $b \in B$, $c \in C$, and deduce that $B \cup C$ is a basis of order $2$ with counting function $O(\sqrt{x})$.
